summary: A comment from BBN that the Terminal IMP cannot directly use the proposed mailbox protocol. It cannot store incoming messages for later printing, is not expected to act as a server, and cannot run programs to process varied input. Another host would have to do those jobs for terminals attached to it.

plainLanguage.summary: A small machine says it cannot take part in the mailbox plan because it has nowhere to keep letters and can only act as a visitor, not a host.

questions: why terminal imp could not use mailbox protocol
subtitle: Why small machines cannot run the mailbox protocol.

tldr.problem: A proposed mailbox protocol for network email assumes all machines can store messages and act as servers, but Terminal IMPs (small, simple machines) cannot do either.
tldr.mechanism: BBN proposes that Terminal IMP sites should be able to rent mailboxes at larger hosts, with mail forwarded and retrieved via Telnet.
tldr.outcome: This solution lets Terminal IMP users participate in network mail without requiring local storage or server capability.

today: RFC 224 is a historical comment on an early email protocol design. The rented mailbox concept it proposes anticipates much later email architecture where messages are stored centrally and retrieved on demand.

sections.title: Terminal IMP Limitations
sections.content:
RFC 224 is a comment from BBN on the proposed mailbox protocol. The Terminal IMP is a small machine designed for basic network access, particularly for terminals and dial-in users. However, it has three critical limitations:

It cannot store incoming messages for later printing or display. It cannot perform as the server portion of any connection. It cannot provide programs to process varied input streams—it supports Telnet and may support parts of the Data Transfer Protocol, but not File Transfer Protocol, and it will not perform transformations on the data stream.
sections.plainLanguage: A small machine is designed for visitors to connect in and use, not to receive and store mail or to work as a store itself.

sections.title: Rented Mailbox Solution
sections.content:
BBN proposes that Terminal IMP installations be guaranteed the right to rent mailboxes at a larger host site—the Network Information Center is suggested as a candidate. Messages destined for a Terminal IMP user would be shipped to the renting site and stored there according to protocol.

A Terminal IMP user could then periodically log in via Telnet and examine the mailbox. Since examination happens over Telnet, the host containing the mailbox would automatically perform necessary data transformations before sending to the Terminal IMP. This elegantly solves the storage and transformation problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of the small machine keeping the mail, a bigger computer nearby stores it. The user logs in to read their mail, and the bigger computer takes care of putting it in the right format.

sections.title: Why Not Other Approaches
sections.content:
An alternative would be to require each Terminal IMP site to have a dedicated printer for mail. Mail would be transferred in Telnet format to this printer. However, this approach is technically unattractive: a Terminal IMP could accept mail from only one sender at a time, and the transmission rate would be limited to printer speed. A single printer is poor service for Terminal IMPs with widely scattered terminals (such as dial-in terminals distributed over a 10-mile radius).

BBN concludes that renting mailbox storage at one site is more cost-effective and technically superior to providing a dedicated printer at each Terminal IMP site.
sections.plainLanguage: You could put a printer at each small machine, but then only one letter can arrive at a time and it prints at printer speed. Storing mail at a big computer instead is faster and cheaper.
